title: Infodemia: Another enemy for romanian frontline healthcare workers to fight during the covid-19 outbreak
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 126 Romanian frontline healthcare workers (March-April 2020) whose aim is psychological outcomes, but which reports one descriptive share with a denominator: 34% answered yes to 'Are you affected by false news in the course of your professional activity?' (43 of 126, matching the group sizes N1=43 / N2=83 in Table 2). Under the rule that a study with a different aim is still included when a descriptive share is reported, this qualifies as a self-report (RECALL) share. It is nevertheless a self-reported IMPACT rather than an encounter question, so the single row is flagged borderline.

estimates.platform: Survey (channel unspecified; media in general, incl. social media, online press, television)
estimates.measure_type: % of frontline healthcare workers who say they are affected by false news in the course of their professional activity
estimates.value_raw: 34% of frontline healthcare workers answered yes; corresponding group sizes in Table 2 are N1 = 43 (affected by fake news) and N2 = 83 (not affected) of 126, i.e. 43/126 = 34.1%
estimates.denominator: 126 frontline healthcare workers (94 physicians, 32 nurses) from the Emergency and Intensive Care departments of the County Emergency Clinical Hospital Pius Brinzeu, Timisoara, Romania
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'yes' to the custom item 'Are you affected by false news in the course of your professional activity?' (worded 'Are you affected by fake news in the course of your professional activity?' in the Methods). Respondents self-classified; the authors describe the split as based on 'the self-evaluated criteria'.
estimates.misinfo_def: Misinformation, disinformation, and rumors during a health emergency, false preventive measures, fake remedies, conspiracy theories, and other incorrect information may have consequences beyond public health (WHO framing quoted by the authors); infodemic = disseminating information, both accurate and inaccurate, about an important subject, as a disease
estimates.source_quote: Regarding the specific questions related to the false news impact on the frontline medical staff, we obtained the following results: 34% of frontline healthcare workers answered yes to the question: “Are you affected by false news in the course of your professional activity?”.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report on a single author-written yes/no item developed from a focus group with ICU and Emergency staff; no external verification and, as the authors list among the limitations, 'the subjectivity of the cohort classification'
estimates.moderator_quote: A total of 126 health professionals took part in the survey: 32 nurses and 94 physicians were questioned. ... All data were collected online via a link sent by email.
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE: the item asks whether the respondent is AFFECTED by false news at work, not whether they encountered/were exposed to it, so it mixes exposure with self-perceived impact; it is closer to a perceived-impact than a perceived-amount question. Also note the paper contradicts itself in the Discussion ('almost half of the participants were affected by false news') while the Results and Table 2 give 34% (43/126). No time window is attached to the item. Single-hospital voluntary email survey, no response rate reported, so the denominator is a convenience sample of two departments.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted: answers to 'In what way fake news affects you?' - 'the doctor-patient relationship is affected' 23%, 'it affects me emotionally' 30%, 'it creates confusion' 19% of respondents. These describe the mode of impact, not exposure to misinformation, and the denominator is ambiguous (all 126 respondents or only the 43 who said they were affected). (2) Not extracted: the word best describing the media's position toward medical staff - 'appreciation' 33%, 'distorted' 33%, 'objectivity' 15% - a perception of media coverage of clinicians, not a misinformation share. (3) Not extracted: the DASS-21 and ISI scale means by group (stress 7.23 vs 4.71; depression 4.79 vs 3.59; anxiety 3.93 vs 2.61; insomnia 10.86 vs 8.66) - psychological outcomes, scale means, no misinformation share. (4) The paper reports no measure of how much misinformation these workers actually saw, nor any content analysis.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey (link emailed) of 126 frontline healthcare workers - 94 physicians and 32 nurses - in the Emergency and ICU departments of a single hospital (County Emergency Clinical Hospital Pius Brinzeu, Timisoara, Romania), collected March-April 2020; ethics approval no. 170/05.08.2019, written informed consent. No sampling frame size or response rate is reported, so the sample is a convenience one. Instruments: DASS-21 (Cronbach's alpha 0.88 depression, 0.88 anxiety, 0.91 stress) and the Insomnia Severity Index (alpha 0.91), plus three custom fake-news items generated from a focus group with ICU and Emergency staff; the fake-news exposure grouping is entirely self-evaluated with no coding procedure or reliability statistic. Analysis by independent-samples t-tests in SPSS 21. Authors list the cross-sectional design, small sample and subjective cohort classification as limitations.
rob.item6_quote: Therefore, specific questions related to fake news influence on the frontline medical staff were created, such as: “Are you affected by fake news in the course of your professional activity?”, “In what way fake news affects you?”, “What is the word that best describes the media position (print, audiovisual, online press) regarding medical staff during the outbreak of COVID-19?”.
rob.item10_quote: 34% of frontline healthcare workers answered yes to the question: “Are you affected by false news in the course of your professional activity?”.
